title: Savitṛ comes on his golden chariot

words.role: belongs with yāti in the second line: ā … yāti, ‘comes’
words.context: Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara reads it with the verb: «आयाति आगच्छतु»

words.meaning: through the region (of the sky), the space between earth and heaven

words.gram: present middle participle, m. nom. sg.
words.context: with ā: ‘returning’ — Bhāskara: «आवर्तमानः», rising and setting in turn

words.gram: causative present participle, m. nom. sg.
words.meaning: settling, putting each in its place
words.role: describes savitā; governs amṛtam and martyam

words.context: Bhāskara: the gods and their kind, «देवादिलक्षणम्»
Bhāskara glosses it as «हिरण्मयेन» and notes that the form is listed as irregular («निपात्यते»)

words.meaning: Savitṛ, the Impeller, the Sun as the power that sets things in motion

words.gram: preverb, written again with the verb
words.role: with yāti: ‘comes’; the first ā of the verse is the same preverb

words.context: Bhāskara takes it as a wish: «आगच्छतु», ‘may he come’

words.meaning: looking at each in turn, watching over
words.context: Bhāskara: «विविधं पश्यन् हितेन योजयन्», seeing to each and joining it to its good

sandhi.rule: a final n after a short vowel is doubled before a vowel (P. 8.3.32 (ङमो ह्रस्वादचि ङमुण्नित्यम्))
a + ā becomes ā; then -aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o

morphology.note: the old neuter plural in -ā (for later -āni), common in the Ṛgveda.
the preverb stands apart from its verb (tmesis) and is repeated before it; both belong to yāti.

translation.literal: Hither through the true region turning, settling the immortal and the mortal, with the golden chariot Savitṛ the god comes, looking upon the worlds.
translation.readable: Moving through the abiding sky, setting the immortal and the mortal each in its place, Savitṛ the god comes on his golden chariot, watching over every world.

meaning: The first verse of the midday upasthāna, recited standing and facing the Sun. It pictures the Sun as Savitṛ, the god who sets everything going: he travels the sky on a golden chariot, and as he goes he puts gods and mortals each in their place and looks over all the worlds. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā it is the yājyā verse for an offering to Savitṛ in the Rājasūya (TS 3.4.11.2, with Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s viniyoga); the same verse is the second of a hymn to Savitṛ in the Ṛgveda (1.35.2). At midday the worshipper stands before the Sun at the top of its course, and the verse describes exactly that: the god overseeing everything below.
in_the_rite: Midday sūryopasthāna, first of the five mantras (ā satyena, ud vayam, ud u tyam, citraṃ devānām, tac cakṣuḥ). The Mylapore prayoga gives its viniyoga as Hiraṇyagarbha the seer, triṣṭubh the metre, Savitṛ the deity, used in the upasthāna of the Sun (vin-a-satyena).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara, on TS 3.4.11, reads the verse as a prayer for Savitṛ’s coming: «सविता देवः», «भुवना भुवनानि भूतजातानि विपश्यन् विविधं पश्यन् हितेन योजयन् आयाति आगच्छतु». ‘Real’ is ‘everlasting’ («सत्येन नित्येन»), the region is the world of light, the Sun’s disc («रजसा लोकेन ज्योतिर्मयेन मण्डलात्मना»), and ‘turning’ is the daily round of rising and setting («उदयमस्तमयं चानुपूर्व्येण कुर्वाणः»).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: In the Saṃhitā the verse is the yājyā of the offering to Savitṛ: «तत्रैव याज्या - आ सत्येनेति त्रिष्टुप्».

notes.label: linguistic
notes.text: The verse is a triṣṭubh (eleven syllables to the pāda). The Taittirīya and the Ṛgveda (1.35.2) have the same words; the difference is only spelling and the accent marks of the two traditions.
